bill_summary: This bill updates the Public Local Laws of St. Mary’s County concerning the St. Mary’s County Metropolitan Commission (MetCom). It requires MetCom to receive approval from the St. Mary’s County Commissioners prior to submitting loan applications that incur debt backed by the county's full faith and credit (excluding refinancing with no additional liability), defines 'new facility', updates the definition of 'service area', establishes notice and hearing requirements for new facility plans, and allows MetCom to pay in full or in part for moving utility obstructions based on a prior rights determination.
responsible_party: St. Mary's County Metropolitan Commission
stakeholders: Property owners, residents, and utility infrastructure operators in St. Mary's County served or impacted by public water and sewerage systems.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no state fiscal impact and does not materially affect St. Mary's County operations or finances. MetCom indicated the bill's provisions are procedural in nature and streamline existing practices, noting that MetCom pays all debts it incurs while the county provides full faith and credit backing.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill relates to public water and sewerage systems and aligns definitions with the county comprehensive water and sewerage plan, which falls under the broader regulatory oversight of the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) regarding environmental infrastructure and water quality standards.

The bill updates tax exemption provisions regarding excess revenue derived from the sale or transfer of debt issued by the St. Mary's County Metropolitan Commission from State taxation, which falls under the tax administration responsibilities of the Comptroller.

Synopsis: Altering the application requirements for the homeowners' tax credit to allow homeowners with certain types of income to file an application every 3 years, subject to a certain certification requirement; and applying the Act to all taxable years beginning after June 30, 2023.
Title: Homeowners' Property Tax Credit - Qualified Homeowner - Application and Certification Requirements
bill_summary: Alters the application requirements for Maryland's Homeowners' Property Tax Credit program for qualified homeowners whose only gross income is from Social Security, pensions, or annuities. Qualified homeowners are required to file a complete application in the initial year and every third year thereafter, and may submit a simplified certification in the intervening two years confirming their residency, income sources, and household composition without providing additional proof of income.
responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Homeowners who receive income solely from Social Security, pensions, or annuities and apply for the Homeowners' Property Tax Credit.
fiscal_impact_summary: No state or local fiscal impact. The State Department of Assessments and Taxation can implement the streamlined certification process using existing budgeted resources, as the total number of credit applicants is not expected to significantly change.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board (PTAAB) hears administrative appeals regarding property tax disputes, including denials or determinations regarding property tax credits administered by the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT). The bill modifies application and certification requirements for the Homeowners' Property Tax Credit.

The Maryland Tax Court acts as the highest administrative body hearing appeals regarding property and tax credit determinations arising from the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board and state taxing authorities.

Synopsis: Establishing that a hernia caused as a result of repetitive trauma may be considered an occupational disease and be compensable subject to certain provisions of the workers' compensation law.
Title: Labor and Employment - Workers' Compensation - Hernia

NarrowSubjects.Name: Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- Col Bar; Holiday; etc

bill_summary: Establishes that a hernia caused by repetitive trauma may be considered an occupational disease and compensable under Maryland workers' compensation law.
responsible_party: Workers' Compensation Commission
stakeholders: Covered employees experiencing repetitive trauma hernias, employers, and workers' compensation insurers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect State, local government, or Chesapeake Employers' Insurance Company operations or finances because repetitive trauma hernias are relatively rare and employees are still required to prove the injury is work-related.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Workers' Compensation Commission is the primary agency responsible for administering Maryland's workers' compensation laws and adjudicating claims. This bill directly amends the Labor and Employment Article regarding compensable hernia claims arising from repetitive trauma.

Known as the Chesapeake Employers' Insurance Company, the Injured Workers' Insurance Fund is the third-party administrator of workers' compensation claims for State of Maryland employees and a primary insurer evaluated in the bill's fiscal note regarding the potential impact of repetitive trauma hernia claims.

The Subsequent Injury Fund reviews and investigates workers' compensation claims involving combined effects of pre-existing conditions and work injuries, and was consulted as an informational source regarding the potential compensability of repetitive trauma hernia claims.

Synopsis: Altering a certain condition under which the Board of License Commissioners of Garrett County may issue a certain alcoholic beverages license to a hotel or motel; authorizing a gift basket permit holder to purchase certain alcoholic beverages from a wholesaler; authorizing a holder of a Class C multiple day beer license, beer and wine license, or beer, wine, and liquor license to hold another license that is issued by the Board; etc.
Title: Garrett County Alcoholic Beverages Act of 2023
bill_summary: This bill updates Garrett County alcoholic beverages laws by establishing a framework for license expiration and hardship extensions, lowering the minimum room requirement for hotel/motel Class B licenses from 25 to 10 rooms, allowing gift basket permit holders to purchase alcohol from wholesalers, permitting holders of Class C multiple day and multiple event licenses to hold other licenses of a different class, and expanding Sunday sales hours to begin at 6:00 a.m. instead of 10:00 a.m.
responsible_party: Garrett County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Garrett County alcoholic beverages license holders, hotels and motels, gift basket businesses, clubs holding multiple day or multiple event licenses, and local consumers.
fiscal_impact_summary: State effect is none, as the Judiciary can handle any associated workload with existing resources. Local finances and operations in Garrett County are not materially affected. Affected small businesses may experience increased sales due to the extension of Sunday sale hours.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill addresses the expiration and judicial review of decisions by the Garrett County Board of License Commissioners, and eliminates the need for circuit court approval for extensions due to casualty loss. The fiscal note confirms that the Judiciary / Administrative Office of the Courts can absorb any minor judicial workload impact within existing resources.

Synopsis: Making permanent the Community Solar Energy Generating Systems Pilot Program; requiring a community solar energy generating system to serve at least 40% of its kilowatt-hour output to low-income and moderate-income subscribers under certain circumstances; authorizing a subscription coordinator to act on behalf of a subscriber organization; altering requirements related to the siting and size of certain community solar energy generating systems projects; authorizing the use of consolidated billing for certain charges; etc.
Title: Electricity - Community Solar Energy Generating Systems Program and Property Taxes

Environmental Matters -see also- Conserv; Nat Resrce; Pollut

bill_summary: Makes the Community Solar Energy Generating Systems Pilot Program permanent, adjusts project capacity limits, expands eligible siting, and requires systems to allocate at least 40% of their output to low- and moderate-income subscribers. The bill also authorizes consolidated billing, requires prevailing wage or project labor agreements for projects over 1 megawatt, and extends personal property tax exemptions for qualifying community solar projects.
responsible_party: Public Service Commission
stakeholders: Community solar developers and subscriber organizations, electric companies, electricity customers, low- and moderate-income households, and construction workers.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund expenditures for the Public Service Commission increase by $264,900 in FY 2024, $297,500 in FY 2025, $206,100 in FY 2026, $215,100 in FY 2027, and $226,200 in FY 2028 to cover personnel and consultant costs. Special fund revenues increase correspondingly from assessments imposed on public service companies. Local government personal property tax revenues may decrease beginning in FY 2026 due to the extended exemption period.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: PSC is the primary regulatory and implementing agency responsible for making the Community Solar Energy Generating Systems Program permanent. The bill requires PSC to establish a stakeholder workgroup, adopt and revise program regulations, approve electric company tariffs, implement consolidated billing protocols, oversee net metering capacity, and adds a dedicated full-time position.

The bill requires developers of community solar systems with capacities exceeding 1 MW to pay workers not less than the prevailing wage rate determined under Title 17, Subtitle 2 of the State Finance and Procurement Article, which is administered and enforced by the Maryland Department of Labor.

As the advocate for residential utility customers before the PSC, OPC is directly interested in the consumer protections, electric utility tariffs, consolidated billing changes, and rate impacts on residential ratepayers resulting from the permanent community solar program.

The bill codifies definitions and exemptions for agrivoltaics (combining solar power generation with agriculture) and explicitly identifies agricultural activities as recognized by the Maryland Department of Agriculture.

The bill requires system developers to address Critical Area and forest conservation concerns by complying with the Forest Conservation Act and environmental laws pertaining to Critical Areas, which are under DNR's natural resources statutory framework.

The bill incorporates statutory definitions of 'overburdened community' and 'underserved community' from the Environment Article to establish low- and moderate-income subscriber eligibility, and includes brownfield sites and closed landfills regulated under MDE refuse disposal permits in project siting exemptions.

Synopsis: Continuing the State Commission of Real Estate Appraisers, Appraisal Management Companies, and Home Inspectors in accordance with the provisions of the Maryland Program Evaluation Act (sunset law) by extending to July 1, 2026, the termination provisions relating to certain statutory and regulatory authority of the Commission; and requiring an independent evaluation of the Commission to be conducted in consultation with the Office of Program Evaluation and Government Accountability in the Department of Legislative Services.
Title: State Commission of Real Estate Appraisers, Appraisal Management Companies, and Home Inspectors - Sunset Extension

NarrowSubjects.Name: Real Estate -see also- Agents and Brokers

bill_summary: This bill extends the termination date of the State Commission of Real Estate Appraisers, Appraisal Management Companies, and Home Inspectors by three years, from July 1, 2023, to July 1, 2026. It also requires the Maryland Department of Labor to hire a consultant to conduct an independent evaluation assessing whether the Commission adheres to diversity, equity, and inclusion guidelines under the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Labor
stakeholders: Licensed real estate appraisers, appraisal management companies, home inspectors, and Maryland property buyers and sellers.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund expenditures increase by between $50,000 and $75,000 in FY 2024 only to hire an independent consultant for the required evaluation. Special fund revenues and expenditures for the Commission are otherwise maintained from FY 2024 through FY 2026 due to the sunset extension. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 909 directly affects the Maryland Department of Labor by extending the statutory sunset date for the State Commission of Real Estate Appraisers, Appraisal Management Companies, and Home Inspectors, which operates within the department. Additionally, the department is mandated to hire a consultant and submit an independent evaluation regarding diversity, equity, and inclusion guidelines, incurring special fund expenditures.

Synopsis: Requiring the Public Service Commission to establish certain targets for the deployment of new energy storage devices in the State; requiring the Commission to establish and implement the Maryland Energy Storage Program to meet certain energy storage goals and develop a certain energy storage system in the State; and requiring the Commission to submit a certain report to the General Assembly by December 31, 2023, regarding the implementation of the Maryland Energy Storage Program and any needed statutory changes.
Title: Energy Storage - Targets and Maryland Energy Storage Program - Establishment

NarrowSubjects.Name: Clean Energy Credits -see also- Renewable Energy Sources
Energy Matters -see also- Ren.Energy Sou; Fuel; Power Plants
Utilities -see also- High Voltage Lines; Telephones; Water

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Public Service Commission to establish targets for deploying cost-effective energy storage devices in Maryland—reaching up to 3,000 megawatts of cumulative storage capacity by the end of delivery year 2033—and to implement the Maryland Energy Storage Program by July 1, 2025.
responsible_party: Maryland Public Service Commission
stakeholders: Investor-owned electric companies, energy storage developers and suppliers, electricity consumers and ratepayers, small businesses, and state and local government entities paying electricity rates.
fiscal_impact_summary: Special fund expenditures for the Public Service Commission increase by $649,600 in FY 2025 to hire six additional staff members to administer the program, with costs rising to $700,200 by FY 2028; special fund revenues increase correspondingly via assessments on public service companies. Additionally, State and local government electricity expenditures are anticipated to increase beginning as early as FY 2025 as utilities recover energy storage compliance and incentive costs through customer rates.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the Public Service Commission to establish deployment targets for new energy storage devices, implement the Maryland Energy Storage Program by July 1, 2025, conduct rulemakings, and submit a report to the General Assembly by December 31, 2023. The fiscal note also specifies that the PSC requires six new positions and over $649,000 in special fund expenditures beginning in FY 2025.

The Office of the People's Counsel represents residential utility ratepayers in Public Service Commission proceedings. Because the bill establishes significant procurement mechanisms and potential utility cost-recovery through retail electricity rates for up to 3,000 MW of energy storage, the agency will be engaged in the regulatory design and cost-effectiveness proceedings before the PSC.
The Maryland Energy Administration coordinates statewide energy planning and policy, administers clean energy programs and grants, and monitors energy storage initiatives alongside the PSC.

Synopsis: Requiring student financing companies to register with the Commissioner of Financial Regulation before providing services in the State; requiring a student financing company to renew its registration on an annual basis; authorizing the Commissioner to adopt registration procedures for student financing companies, which may include certain fees; and requiring student financing companies to annually report certain information, to be made publicly accessible on a certain website, to the Commissioner beginning March 15, 2024.
Title: Financial Institutions - Student Financing Companies - Required Registration and Reporting

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties
Debt Collection -see also- Attachments and Garnishments
Higher Education -see also- Comm Colleges; Med Schools; etc.
Investigations and Inquiries -see also- Crim Bckgrnd Invest

bill_summary: This bill requires student financing companies that secure, make, extend, acquire, or assume student financing products to register annually with the Commissioner of Financial Regulation starting March 15, 2024, and to report detailed annual lending, default, and demographic data. It directs the Commissioner to publish this information on a public website, authorizes enforcement and investigation by the Commissioner, the Attorney General, and local State's Attorneys, and voids student financing products if a company knowingly violates registration or reporting requirements.
responsible_party: Commissioner of Financial Regulation in the Maryland Department of Labor
stakeholders: Student financing companies, postsecondary educational institutions providing financing, and Maryland consumers and students using or refinancing private student financing products.
fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not materially affected. The Office of the Commissioner of Financial Regulation (OCFR) can implement the bill's registration, reporting, and regulatory requirements with existing budgeted resources. Revenues are likely not materially affected because registration and renewal fees may be paid directly to a third-party licensing system (NMLS). Local government operations and finances are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill assigns primary implementation and enforcement authority to the Commissioner of Financial Regulation, which is housed within the Department of Labor. The Commissioner is responsible for establishing registration and reporting procedures for student financing companies, maintaining a public registry/database, adopting regulations, and conducting enforcement actions.

The bill explicitly authorizes the Attorney General to enforce the registration and reporting requirements using the same investigative and enforcement powers granted to the Commissioner of Financial Regulation.
The bill renders non-compliant student financing contracts void and unenforceable and may involve circuit courts in subpoena enforcement and judicial review of administrative actions.

Synopsis: Clarifying that a certain proceeding for judicial review of a final decision or order by the Public Service Commission may be instituted in a circuit court for a county in which the public service company that is a party to the proceeding provides service or in the Circuit Court for Baltimore City.
Title: Public Service Commission – Judicial Review – Proceedings
bill_summary: Clarifies venue requirements for judicial review of a final decision or order of the Public Service Commission, specifying that proceedings must be filed in the Circuit Court for Baltimore City or in a circuit court for a county where the public service company that was a party to the proceeding provides service.
responsible_party: Public Service Commission
stakeholders: Public service companies, parties or persons in interest appealing PSC orders (including the Office of People's Counsel, Department of Natural Resources, and Department of the Environment), and the circuit courts.
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local finances and operations are not materially affected. However, Public Service Commission administrative expenditures may decrease or be reallocated due to reduced travel for legal staff from limited judicial review venues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly governs the venue for judicial review proceedings of final decisions or orders issued by the Public Service Commission, which may reduce administrative and travel expenditures for PSC legal counsel.

The Office of the People's Counsel represents residential utility consumers in proceedings before the PSC and in court appeals, and is specifically authorized to seek judicial review under the amended statute.
The bill amends venue requirements specifying which circuit courts have jurisdiction to receive and hear petitions for judicial review of PSC decisions.
The Secretary of Natural Resources is statutorily authorized under the cross-referenced section to seek judicial review of PSC decisions relating to power plant siting.
The Secretary of the Environment holds statutory authority under the cross-referenced section to seek judicial review of certain environmental decisions made by the PSC.
The statute cross-references actions where the Motor Vehicle Administration suspends or revokes carrier registrations in accordance with PSC orders subject to judicial review.

Synopsis: Establishing procedures for the Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore City, in the case of an alleged complaint against a licensed establishment or license holder, to make an offer of a monetary penalty as a compromise in lieu of a hearing before the Board under certain circumstances; and altering the maximum penalty for certain alcoholic beverages violations.
Title: Baltimore City - Alcoholic Beverages - Violation Procedures and Fines

NarrowSubjects.Name: Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

bill_summary: Authorizes the Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore City to offer a monetary penalty as a compromise in lieu of a hearing to an alcoholic beverages license holder facing an alleged violation. It also raises the maximum fine from $3,000 to $20,000 for subsequent offenses that are cause for license suspension and for operating or promoting an unauthorized pub crawl.
responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore City
stakeholders: Alcoholic beverages license holders, licensed establishments, and pub crawl promoters in Baltimore City.
fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are unaffected. Baltimore City revenues may potentially increase due to the collection of monetary penalties under offers of compromise and the increase in maximum fines from $3,000 to $20,000 for certain violations. Implementation of procedural requirements can be handled using the Board's existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Alcoholic Beverages Article regarding violation compromise procedures and fine limits administered locally by the Baltimore City Board of License Commissioners. While the fiscal note indicates no state fiscal impact, the Comptroller is the primary state authority identified as regulating the alcohol industry in Maryland.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore City to approve a license expansion to a noncontiguous property with a second separate use permit issued by the City if a certain condition is met; authorizing the establishment and conversion of various alcoholic beverages licenses in the 46th alcoholic beverages district; extending for 1 year the expiration of an alcoholic beverage licenses issued for  certain areas for certain transferal and renewal purposes; etc.
Title: Baltimore City - Alcoholic Beverages - 46th Alcoholic Beverages District - Revisions

NarrowSubjects.Name: Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes; Reimb Rates

bill_summary: This bill revises alcoholic beverages laws in Baltimore City, primarily within the 46th alcoholic beverages district. It authorizes the Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore City to approve premises expansions onto noncontiguous properties for certain nonprofit-operated restaurants, permits the issuance of new Class B beer, wine, and liquor licenses in specified areas under certain conditions, and establishes a process allowing eligible Class D beer and light wine license holders to convert to Class D beer, wine, and liquor licenses upon payment of a $15,000 fee. It also adjusts seating capacity exceptions for license transfers in ward 3, precinct 3, alters Baltimore City Charter requirements regarding police patrol contracts, and temporarily extends the expiration date of certain licenses until July 1, 2024, for transfer or renewal.
responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore City
stakeholders: Alcoholic beverage licensees, restaurant and bar owners, license applicants in Baltimore City's 46th district, local community associations, and restaurant patrons.
fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not affected. Baltimore City revenues may increase minimally beginning in FY 2024 from license application fees, renewal fees, annual license fees, and a $15,000 special transfer fee for qualifying Class D license conversions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland regulates the state's alcohol industry and oversees state alcohol taxation. Although this bill primarily concerns local alcoholic beverage licenses administered by the Baltimore City Board of License Commissioners with no direct state fiscal impact, it relates to the broader statutory framework governing alcoholic beverages in Maryland.

Synopsis: Establishing consumer protections related to the repair or replacement of motor vehicle glass on motor vehicles equipped with an advanced driver assistance system; and establishing that a violation of the Act is an unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practice.
Title: Consumer Protection - Motor Vehicle Glass Repair or Replacement - Advanced Driver Assistance System Recalibration

NarrowSubjects.Name: Consumer Protection -see also- Unfair Trade Practices
Motor Vehicles -see also- Aband Veh; Ambulances; Buses; etc.
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

bill_summary: Establishes consumer protections regarding the repair or replacement of motor vehicle glass on vehicles equipped with an advanced driver assistance system (ADAS). It requires safety glass facilities to inform customers if recalibration is required, provide a written statement that the work will meet or exceed manufacturer specifications, refrain from charging for unperformed or incomplete services, and notify customers if recalibration was required but not completed. Violations are classified as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act.
responsible_party: Office of the Attorney General (Consumer Protection Division)
stakeholders: Motor vehicle owners with vehicles equipped with advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS), and motor vehicle safety glass repair and replacement facilities.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not have a material impact on State or local government finances or operations. The Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General can implement and enforce the requirements using existing resources, and the small business effect is minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes consumer protection standards for motor vehicle safety glass facilities regarding advanced driver assistance system recalibration and makes violations an unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practice under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act, which is enforced by the Office of the Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division.

Synopsis: Prohibiting the Department of Commerce from denying certain cannabis business entities conducting business in the State certain economic development program benefits under certain circumstances; clarifying the eligibility of certain cannabis business entities conducting business in the State under the Job Creation and One Maryland programs; authorizing certain cannabis business entities to reapply for benefits under certain economic development programs; etc.
Title: Economic Development - Program Participation - Cannabis Business Establishments

NarrowSubjects.Name: Cannabis Distribution -see also- Cannabis, Cannabis Prod.
Cannabis Production -see also- Cannabis, Cannabis Dist.
Commerce and Business -see also- Dealers; Elec. Comm.; etc.
Licenses -see also- AB Lic; Certifications;Drivers' Licenses

bill_summary: Prohibits the Department of Commerce from denying state-licensed cannabis business entities economic development and financial assistance program benefits solely due to their status as cannabis establishments, allows previously denied cannabis businesses to reapply, and explicitly designates the growth, processing, or dispensing of cannabis as eligible business activities under the Job Creation and One Maryland tax credit programs.
responsible_party: Department of Commerce
stakeholders: State-licensed cannabis business entities (growers, processors, and dispensaries), small business owners in the cannabis industry, and local governments receiving highway user revenues.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues decrease, potentially significantly, beginning in FY 2025 to the extent newly eligible cannabis dispensaries claim Job Creation (capped at $4.0 million annually) and One Maryland tax credits (up to $5.0 million per credit, with no annual cap). Special fund revenues (Transportation Trust Fund and Higher Education Investment Fund) and local highway user revenues decrease if credits are claimed against corporate income taxes. Prohibiting denial of program benefits conforms to Commerce's existing practice and has no direct operational expenditure impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Economic Development Article to prohibit the Department of Commerce from denying economic development program benefits to licensed cannabis businesses, and broadens eligibility for major programs administered by Commerce, including the Job Creation, One Maryland, and More Jobs for Marylanders tax credit programs.

As the state's tax collector, the Comptroller processes and administers the corporate and personal income tax credits expanded under the bill (Job Creation and One Maryland tax credits) and experiences revenue impacts resulting from those claims.

The agency licenses and regulates the cannabis growers, processors, and dispensaries that are granted statutory protection and eligibility for state economic development programs and tax credits under the bill.
The Transportation Trust Fund (TTF) administered for MDOT experiences an indirect reduction in corporate income tax distributions resulting from the expanded tax credits claimed under the bill.

Synopsis: Providing that the Secretary of Higher Education is appointed by and serves at the pleasure of the Governor; requiring each institution of higher education to adopt a written policy that provides reasonable academic accommodations for students to practice sincerely held faith-based or religious beliefs; altering eligibility criteria for and the process for awards from the Delegate Howard P. Rawlings Program of Educational Excellence Awards; altering the administration of the Maryland Community College Promise Scholarship; etc.
Title: Higher Education - Appointment of Secretary and Student Financial Assistance - Accommodations at Public Institutions for Religious Beliefs

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties
Higher Education -see also- Comm Colleges; Med Schools; etc.
Licenses -see also- AB Lic; Certifications;Drivers' Licenses
Salaries and Compensation -see also- Overtime; Reimb. Rates
Secondary Schools -see also- Education; Private/Public Sch.

bill_summary: This bill alters the appointment of the Maryland Secretary of Higher Education so that the Secretary is appointed by and serves at the pleasure of the Governor. It requires public institutions of higher education to adopt religious accommodation policies and provide space on campus for faith-based practices. Additionally, the bill alters eligibility and administration processes for State financial aid programs, transferring the administration of the Maryland Community College Promise Scholarship directly to community colleges and shifting notification and award distribution responsibilities for Guaranteed Access Grants to institutions of higher education starting in 2025.
responsible_party: Maryland Higher Education Commission (MHEC) and its Office of Student Financial Assistance (OSFA), along with Maryland public institutions of higher education and community colleges
stakeholders: College and community college students (including low-income financial aid recipients and students seeking religious accommodations), Maryland public institutions of higher education, community colleges, and participating nonpublic colleges
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $278,200 in FY 2024 for contractual modifications to the Maryland College Aid Processing System (MDCAPS), with possible additional costs in FY 2026. Higher education expenditures at Baltimore City Community College increase beginning in FY 2024 to administer Promise scholarships, and public institutions may incur minimal expenditure increases starting in FY 2026 to implement Guaranteed Access Grant notification systems (which may be offset by future general fund appropriations). Locally funded community colleges incur administrative costs starting in FY 2024 to verify applicant eligibility and distribute Promise scholarship awards, as well as minimal costs beginning in FY 2026 for grant notifications.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MHEC and its Office of Student Financial Assistance (OSFA) are central to the bill, which alters the appointment and tenure of the Secretary of Higher Education, retains OSFA within MHEC rather than spinning it off, and modifies the administration, eligibility, and auditing of major state financial assistance programs including Guaranteed Access Grants, Educational Assistance Grants, and the Community College Promise Scholarship.

As the primary state entity overseeing postsecondary education and student financial aid, the commission is directly impacted by changes to the appointment of the Secretary of Higher Education, the restructuring of financial aid award procedures, and ongoing oversight and auditing responsibilities.

MSDE administers the Next Generation Scholars of Maryland Program, which the bill expands by altering eligibility to include students qualifying for free or reduced-price lunch under the National School Lunch Program and allowing continued participation for students who relocate.

The bill directly amends the Governor's appointment power by authorizing the Governor to appoint the Secretary of Higher Education directly without requiring a list of three nominees from MHEC, and establishes that the Secretary serves at the pleasure of the Governor.

USM constituent institutions are public higher education institutions required under the bill to adopt written policies granting reasonable academic accommodations for faith-based practices, provide dedicated space on campus for religious practices, and take on responsibilities to notify students of and administer Guaranteed Access Grant awards.

As a public institution of higher education, Morgan State University must adopt written policies for faith-based and religious accommodations, provide campus space for religious practices, and implement systems to notify students of and administer Guaranteed Access Grant awards.

As an independent public honors college, St. Mary's College of Maryland must adopt a written policy on religious accommodations, designate space on campus for faith-based practices, and participate in verifying and notifying students of Guaranteed Access Grant awards.

The office supports the Governor in vetting and processing executive appointments, which is directly affected by eliminating MHEC's three-nominee requirement for the appointment of the Secretary of Higher Education.

Synopsis: Altering the hours during which a licensee may sell alcoholic beverages on Sundays in Frederick County.
Title: Frederick County - Alcoholic Beverages - Sunday Sales
bill_summary: This bill extends Sunday sales hours for specified alcoholic beverages licenses in Frederick County—including various Class A, B, and C licenses, conference centers, dinner theaters, entertainment centers, hotel lobbies, and municipal golf courses—generally aligning Sunday hours of sale with weekday hours (typically 6:00 a.m. to 2:00 a.m. the following day).
responsible_party: Frederick County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Alcoholic beverages license holders, restaurants, hotels, clubs, dinner theaters, retail alcohol establishments, and consumers in Frederick County.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no state fiscal impact and does not materially affect Frederick County finances or operations. However, it may have a potentially meaningful positive impact on small businesses by enabling license holders to realize additional sales through expanded Sunday operating hours.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland regulates the state's alcohol industry and oversees state alcohol taxation and licensing frameworks. While HB 939 specifically alters local Sunday operating hours for retail alcoholic beverage licenses in Frederick County with no direct state fiscal impact, it falls broadly under the Comptroller's regulatory area of oversight regarding alcoholic beverages.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Board of License Commissioners for Prince George's County to issue up to five Class B-DD (Development District) beer, wine, and liquor licenses for restaurants located within the Main Street Laurel development.
Title: Prince George's County - Alcoholic Beverages - Main Street Laurel Development PG 404-23
bill_summary: Authorizes the Board of License Commissioners for Prince George's County to issue up to five Class B-DD (Development District) beer, wine, and liquor licenses for restaurants located within a defined area of Main Street Laurel.
responsible_party: Prince George's County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Restaurants located within the Main Street Laurel development area and restaurant patrons in Prince George's County.
fiscal_impact_summary: State effect: None. Local effect: Prince George's County revenues increase by an annual license fee of $3,025 for each Class B-DD license issued (up to $15,125 annually if all five licenses are issued), beginning in FY 2024. County enforcement activities can be handled with existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is responsible for the overarching regulation and enforcement of the state's alcohol industry. However, this legislation specifically authorizes the local Prince George's County Board of License Commissioners to issue local Class B-DD licenses, resulting in minimal state-level involvement and no state fiscal impact.

Synopsis: Authorizing the governing body of Charles County to grant, by law, a  tax credit against the property tax imposed on the owner-occupied residence of certain emergency responders and their surviving spouses if the federal adjusted gross income of the emergency responder or the unmarried surviving spouse for the immediately preceding taxable years is $150,000 or less; and applying the Act to all taxable years beginning after June 30, 2023.
Title: Charles County - Property Tax - Credit for Volunteer Emergency Responders

NarrowSubjects.Name: Laws and Ordinances -see also- Pub Local Laws; Uniform Laws
Rescue Squads -see also- Ambulances; Emergency Medical Serv

bill_summary: Authorizes the governing body of Charles County to establish a local property tax credit for the principal residence of active or retired volunteer emergency responders (fire, rescue, or emergency medical services) or their unmarried surviving spouses, provided their federal adjusted gross income for the preceding taxable year is $150,000 or less.
responsible_party: Charles County Government
stakeholders: Active and retired volunteer emergency responders in Charles County, their unmarried surviving spouses, and the Charles County Government
fiscal_impact_summary: State effect: None. Local effect: To the extent the property tax credit is granted, Charles County property tax revenues decrease by an estimated $347,300 in FY 2024 and $375,900 in FY 2028 (assuming a $500 credit). County expenditures increase by $115,900 in FY 2024 and $130,400 in FY 2028 to hire one additional staff person in the County Treasurer's Office to administer the tax credit.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill authorizes an optional property tax credit in Charles County for volunteer emergency responders. As the administrative appellate body for property tax assessments, exemptions, and credits following local determinations, the Charles County Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board could potentially receive appeals concerning eligibility for this tax credit.

The Maryland Tax Court hears appeals from final decisions of local taxing authorities and Property Tax Assessment Appeals Boards involving real property tax disputes and credits, giving it potential jurisdiction over contested determinations under this credit.

Synopsis: Establishing the Maryland Native Plants Program to respond to the increasing demand for, use of, and sale of native plants at retail garden centers and wholesale nurseries and to educate the public on native plants; requiring the Department of Agriculture to administer the Program in coordination with the University of Maryland Extension and to establish the "Maryland Natives" marketing program; requiring the University of Maryland Extension to hire an extension agent to serve as a native plant specialist for certain purposes; etc.
Title: Maryland Native Plants Program

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- Dealers; Elec. Comm.; etc.
Education -see also- Driver Ed; Higher Ed; Special Ed; etc
Hazardous and Toxic Substances -see also- Asbestos; Radiatn
Higher Education -see also- Comm Colleges; Med Schools; etc.
Natural Resources -see also- Conserv; Forest & Park; Wildlds
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- Col Bar; Holiday; etc

bill_summary: Establishes the Maryland Native Plants Program, administered by the Maryland Department of Agriculture in coordination with the University of Maryland Extension, to promote the sale and use of Maryland native plants. The program requires the creation of a Commercial Maryland Native Plant List, a voluntary certification program for growers and retailers, a 'Maryland Natives' marketing program and logo, a dedicated educational webpage, and the hiring of an Extension agent as a native plant specialist.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Agriculture and University of Maryland Extension
stakeholders: Retail garden centers, wholesale and retail plant nurseries, commercial growers, landscapers, and the general public/plant consumers.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $285,100 in FY 2025 for 2 new positions (one at UME and one at MDA), logo development, and operating expenses, rising to $300,100 by FY 2029. The bill establishes statutory mandated annual appropriations beginning in FY 2025 of $150,000 for UME and $100,000 for MDA ($250,000 total). State revenues and local government finances are unaffected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MDA is the primary administering agency for the Maryland Native Plants Program, responsible for creating the voluntary certification program, developing and maintaining the Commercial Maryland Native Plant List, running the 'Maryland Natives' marketing program, and promoting program resources on its 'Maryland's Best' website, supported by a mandated annual appropriation.

The University of Maryland Extension (part of USM) is tasked with administering the educational components of the program, hiring a dedicated extension agent as a Native Plant Specialist, providing ongoing expertise for plant lists and certifications, and creating a dedicated webpage, backed by a mandated annual appropriation.

DNR is statutorily required to provide input and expertise to MDA regarding the Commercial Maryland Native Plant List, evaluate cultivars and hybrids, and host a link to the program's webpage on its native plants website.

DBM oversees state budget formulation and personnel allocations, which are impacted by the bill's mandated ongoing general fund appropriations of $150,000 for UME and $100,000 for MDA starting in FY 2025.
The bill mandates that the Governor include specific annual appropriations ($150,000 for UME and $100,000 for MDA) in the state budget bill beginning in FY 2025.

Synopsis: Prohibiting the State Department of Assessments and Taxation from disbursing or authorizing the disbursement of certain funds to a county if the county has not provided certain information concerning its tax sales; altering the taxable year for which the Department is required to obtain certain information concerning county tax sales; and applying the Act prospectively.
Title: Tax Sales - Data Collection - County Funding

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties

bill_summary: Prohibits the State Department of Assessments and Taxation from disbursing or authorizing the disbursement of certain funds to a county if the county fails to provide required tax sale data, and changes the reporting timeframe for the tax sale survey to the second immediately preceding taxable year.
responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Maryland counties and local governments conducting tax sales, as well as property owners subject to the tax sale process.

responsible_party: The Governor
stakeholders: Nepali and South Asian communities in Maryland and the general public
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no state or local fiscal impact, as commemorating Dashain Day does not affect government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: House Bill 967 explicitly mandates that the Governor annually proclaim October 5 as Dashain Day.

GOCI houses ethnic and cultural commissions representing Asian American and South Asian American communities, which liaise with the Governor's Office regarding cultural observances and community celebrations such as Dashain.

bill_summary: The Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity Act of 2023 requires the Public Service Commission (PSC) to employ cybersecurity experts to advise commissioners and oversee utility cybersecurity practices. Regulated public service companies (excluding telephone companies and common carriers) must adopt zero-trust approaches and minimum security standards, undergo biennial third-party cybersecurity assessments starting by July 1, 2024, submit compliance certifications to the PSC, and report cybersecurity incidents to the State Security Operations Center in the Department of Information Technology.
responsible_party: Public Service Commission
stakeholders: Regulated public service companies (investor-owned electric, electric cooperatives, municipal electric, gas, and water/sewer companies), utility customers, and cybersecurity assessment contractors.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund expenditures for the Public Service Commission increase by $364,400 in FY 2024 to support three new cybersecurity staff positions, rising to $510,500 by FY 2028. Special fund revenues increase correspondingly via regulatory assessments on public service companies. The Department of Information Technology can absorb responsibilities within existing resources. Local government expenditures for municipal electric utilities increase by an indeterminate but potentially significant amount starting in FY 2024 to perform required biennial third-party cybersecurity assessments and comply with security standards.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the Public Service Commission by requiring it to add cybersecurity experts to its staff, collaborate with the Office of Security Management to establish cybersecurity standards for regulated entities, collect compliance certifications from public service companies, and submit biennial cybersecurity reports to the State Chief Information Security Officer.

The bill directly tasks units within DoIT—specifically the State Chief Information Security Officer (SCISO), the Office of Security Management (OSM), and the State Security Operations Center—with collaborating with the PSC on cybersecurity standards, establishing reporting processes, receiving incident reports from public service companies, and receiving biennial utility cybersecurity reports. The bill also authorizes transfers from the Dedicated Purpose Account to DoIT for cybersecurity capacity.

The Secretary of General Services or the Secretary's designee is a designated member of the Workgroup on Mold Standards and Remediation.
The Secretary of Health or the Secretary's designee is designated as a member of the Workgroup on Mold Standards and Remediation.

The Secretary of Labor or the Secretary's designee is designated as a member of the Workgroup on Mold Standards and Remediation.

The Workgroup on Mold Standards and Remediation is mandated to submit its findings and recommendations to the Governor by October 1, 2024.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner as a unit within the Maryland Department of Health to advance forensic science and perform death investigations. It renames the State Postmortem Examiners Commission to the Postmortem Examiners Advisory Committee, redefining its role to serve in an advisory capacity, and transfers various powers and staffing duties to the Department and the Office. Additionally, it adjusts qualifications and staffing requirements for medical examiners, prohibits the Department and Committee from interfering with clinical autopsy findings, and exempts certain Employees' Pension System retirees reemployed as health care practitioners at the Office from retirement benefit reductions.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Staff of the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner (including medical examiners, pathologists, and toxicologists), members of the Postmortem Examiners Advisory Committee, and retired Employees' Pension System health care practitioners reemployed by the Office.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill's changes are procedural in nature and do not materially affect State or local finances. The pension earnings limitation exemption is expected to apply in very few cases and will not have a material effect on State Retirement and Pension System liabilities or contribution rates.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 977 establishes the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner directly as a unit within the Department of Health, transfers administrative and staffing authority to the department, and authorizes the Secretary of Health to adopt regulations and consult on leadership appointments.

The bill amends State Personnel and Pensions law to exempt Employees' Pension System retirees reemployed on a contractual basis by MDH as health care practitioners in the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner from standard retirement allowance reductions.
The Secretary of Budget and Management is statutorily required to approve the compensation set by MDH for personnel appointed to the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.
The Secretary of State Police is designated by statute as an ex officio member of the Postmortem Examiners Advisory Committee.

The bill continues and renumbers provisions under which appeals regarding the denial of requests to correct medical examiner findings and conclusions on cause or manner of death are referred to the Office of Administrative Hearings for contested case proceedings.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill transitions the State Postmortem Examiners Commission into an advisory body named the Postmortem Examiners Advisory Committee, outlining its ongoing membership, meeting procedures, and advisory responsibilities.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Pilot Program for Human Services Careers and the companion Pilot Program for Human Services Careers Scholarship to assist high school students and current Department of Human Services (DHS) employees in Baltimore City, Baltimore County, and Prince George's County in pursuing careers in targeted DHS positions. It also expands eligibility for the Maryland Loan Assistance Repayment Program (LARP) for Police Officers and the Maryland Police Officers Scholarship Program to include parole and probation agents employed by the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services, adjusting mandated appropriations between the two programs. In addition, it requires the State to provide a matching employer contribution of up to $600 annually to eligible State employees participating in State supplemental retirement plans or making qualifying higher education loan payments.
responsible_party: Department of Human Services and Maryland Higher Education Commission
stakeholders: State employees participating in supplemental retirement plans or repaying student loans; parole and probation agents; high school students and public school systems in Baltimore City, Baltimore County, and Prince George's County; and current DHS employees in targeted career tracks.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures increase by an estimated $21.8 million in FY 2024 and $21.7 million annually thereafter, comprising $13.5 million in general funds, $4.1 million in special funds, and $4.1 million in federal funds. This covers $20.6 million for State supplemental retirement matching contributions, $1.0 million for new scholarships, $120,723 in administrative and personnel costs for the Maryland Higher Education Commission, and $50,000 for DHS participant stipends. The bill shifts $3.5 million in annual mandated general fund appropriations from the police scholarship program to the police and probation agent loan assistance repayment program, resulting in a net-zero change to mandated funding. Supplemental retirement plan special fund revenues increase minimally from account fees. Local school systems in the three eligible jurisdictions may incur indeterminate costs to update course curricula.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Pilot Program for Human Services Careers within DHS, requiring the department to collaborate with local school systems, award $500 stipends, establish mentorship programs, select scholarship recipients, and report to the General Assembly.

MHEC is tasked with administering the new Pilot Program for Human Services Careers Scholarship, updating the MDCAPS system, and administering the expanded Maryland Loan Assistance Repayment Program and Scholarship Program for Police Officers and Probation Agents.

MHEC is directly responsible for implementing the new Pilot Program for Human Services Careers Scholarship as well as administering the modified loan repayment and scholarship programs that now include probation agents.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Teachers & State Employees Supplemental Retirement Plans
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates that the State provide an employer matching contribution of up to $600 per fiscal year to participating employees in State supplemental retirement plans administered by MSRP, which increases assets under management and generates fee revenue for the agency.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill expands eligibility for both the Maryland Loan Assistance Repayment Program and the Police Officers Scholarship Program to include DPSCS parole and probation agents, supervisors, and regional administrators.

As the principal agency managing state employee personnel, benefits, and the state budget, DBM is impacted by the $20.6 million annual requirement for state employer matching contributions for employee supplemental retirement accounts.

The bill alters the funding and structure of the Maryland Police Officers Scholarship Program and Loan Assistance Repayment Program by expanding the applicant pool to probation agents and shifting $3.5 million from the scholarship program to LARP.

The bill amends the Education Article to mandate local school system participation, curriculum changes, and career counseling regarding DHS career pathways in three jurisdictions overseen within the state education framework.
The scholarship programs and loan repayment programs apply to students enrolled at public senior higher education institutions in Maryland, including USM constituent institutions.
The bill alters statutory mandated appropriations that the Governor must include in the annual state budget for police and probation officer scholarship and loan repayment programs.

bill_summary: House Bill 983 establishes the Wildlife Conservation, Education, and Outreach Program within the Department of Natural Resources to promote outdoor recreation, stewardship, hunting, and wildlife conservation. The bill increases fees for various hunting and trapping licenses, permits, and stamps, establishes resident and nonresident sika deer stamps, allows eligible nonresident college students in Maryland to purchase resident hunting licenses, and expands the Heritage Conservation Fund to include acquiring land for public hunting. Additionally, it directs the Department of Natural Resources to formulate a deer overpopulation plan in consultation with the Department of Agriculture and to allocate a portion of increased federal funding to eight new department personnel positions and a farmer cost-share forage crop program.
responsible_party: Department of Natural Resources
stakeholders: Hunters, trappers, nonresident college students in Maryland, agricultural landowners and farmers, veterans, and youth and suburban/exurban community members participating in outdoor recreation and conservation programs.
fiscal_impact_summary: Special fund revenues to the Wildlife Management and Protection Fund increase by an estimated $2,271,600 annually beginning in FY 2024 due to increased fees and new stamps. Special fund expenditures increase correspondingly by $2,271,600 annually starting in FY 2024 for administrative expenses (including hiring eight staff positions totaling $938,068 in FY 2024) and conservation projects. Federal fund grant matching revenues increase by an estimated $6,814,900 annually starting in FY 2025, with federal expenditures increasing by at least $563,916 in FY 2025 for ongoing staff costs and funding for a farmer cost-share program. Local government operations and finances are not directly affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DNR is the primary implementing agency responsible for administering the Wildlife Conservation, Education, and Outreach Program, adjusting hunting and trapping license/stamp fees, administering the Wildlife Management and Protection Fund and Heritage Conservation Fund, creating eight new staff positions, establishing a farmer cost-share program, and developing a statewide deer overpopulation plan.

The bill explicitly requires DNR to consult with the Maryland Department of Agriculture to develop a plan addressing deer overpopulation in the state, and establishes a farmer cost-share program to mitigate wildlife crop damage on agricultural land.

The bill mandates the creation of eight new state Position Identification Numbers (PINs) for DNR personnel funded by federal matching funds and involves substantial special and federal fund expenditure adjustments overseen by DBM.
The Treasurer is designated in statute to receive, account for, and credit stamp and licensing fees to the State Wildlife Management and Protection Fund.

bill_summary: The Public Employee Relations Act consolidates Maryland's collective bargaining laws for State, public school, higher education, and community college employees into a unified framework under the State Government Article. It repeals the State Labor Relations Board, State Higher Education Labor Relations Board, and Public School Labor Relations Board, replacing them with a newly established Public Employee Relations Board (PERB) to oversee bargaining units, union elections, dispute resolutions, and unfair labor practice proceedings.
responsible_party: The newly established Public Employee Relations Board (PERB)
stakeholders: Maryland public employees (including State employees, public school system employees, community college employees, and higher education personnel), public employers, and certified employee organizations (unions).
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by at least $642,600 in FY 2024 to support new staff positions, member stipends, a full-time board chair salary, and operating costs for the newly created Public Employee Relations Board (rising to $888,400 by FY 2028). The State may also achieve certain administrative efficiencies from board consolidation. State revenues and local government expenditures are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Public Employee Relations Board as an independent unit of State government to oversee collective bargaining for public employees, conduct representation elections, and adjudicate unfair labor practices.
The bill repeals the Public School Labor Relations Board and transfers its statutory responsibilities, authority, and pending proceedings to the newly established Public Employee Relations Board.

agency_relevance.agency_name: State Higher Education Labor Relations Board
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill repeals the State Higher Education Labor Relations Board and transfers its statutory responsibilities, authority, and pending proceedings to the newly established Public Employee Relations Board.

As the State's central personnel agency, DBM oversees executive branch employee relations, bargaining unit assignments, and the implementation of collective bargaining agreements and statewide personnel policies restructured under the bill.
The bill designates the Office of Administrative Hearings as a venue authorized to conduct hearings regarding unfair labor practice complaints issued by the Board.

The Governor is responsible for appointing all five members of the newly created Public Employee Relations Board (including the chair) with the advice and consent of the Senate, and retains the authority to remove members for incompetence or misconduct.

USM and its constituent institutions are public employers subject to the consolidated collective bargaining provisions, with statutory mandates regarding separate bargaining units and unit classification assignments by institution presidents.
Morgan State University is a covered public employer under the bill, with provisions specifically addressing separate bargaining units and governing board authority over classification assignments.

St. Mary's College of Maryland is explicitly governed by the collective bargaining provisions and is required to maintain separate bargaining units with classification authority held by its governing board.
The bill explicitly defines faculty at the Maryland School for the Deaf and mandates a separate, dedicated bargaining unit for them.
The bill statutorily requires a separate bargaining unit specifically for Maryland Transportation Authority police officers at the rank of first sergeant and below.

The OAG provides legal counsel and representation to the newly created Board, and the fiscal note notes that additional assistant Attorneys General will be required to support PERB's expanded enforcement and subpoena powers.
The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in recruiting, vetting, and managing nominations for the newly established seats on the Public Employee Relations Board.
The bill explicitly references the Maryland Environmental Service regarding collective bargaining negotiations, employer rights, and statutory compliance.

bill_summary: Authorizes students who are at least 18 years old but under the legal drinking age to taste, but not swallow, alcoholic beverages as part of educational coursework in enology, fermenting, brewing, or hospitality and tourism at qualified institutions of higher education without criminal penalty.
responsible_party: Alcohol and Tobacco Commission
stakeholders: Undergraduate students aged 18 to 20 enrolled in enology, brewing, fermenting, or hospitality and tourism programs, course instructors, and qualified postsecondary institutions in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to affect State or local government operations or finances, and qualified institutions are not required to obtain a license or permit provided no extra fee is charged for tastings.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MHEC is the state's coordinating board for postsecondary education, overseeing academic programs and policies across Maryland colleges and universities that may offer coursework in enology, brewing, fermentation, or hospitality.

USM oversees public universities in Maryland, several of which offer degree and certificate programs in fermentation science, agriculture, and hospitality that are directly impacted by allowing eligible students under 21 to taste alcoholic beverages for instructional purposes.

The Comptroller regulates the state's alcoholic beverage industry; the bill amends the Alcoholic Beverages Article and exempts qualified higher education institutions from needing an alcoholic beverage license or permit to conduct instructional tastings.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the Maryland Family and Medical Leave Insurance (FAMLI) Program by delaying the start of required contributions to October 1, 2024, and benefit payments to January 1, 2026. It establishes a 50/50 cost-sharing split between employers and employees, caps the total contribution rate at 1.2% of wages up to the Social Security wage base, repeals the mandate requiring employees to exhaust employer-provided leave before receiving FAMLI benefits, and requires the Maryland Department of Health to reimburse certain community service providers for employer contributions.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Labor and Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Maryland employees, employers with 15 or more employees, self-employed participants, and licensed community healthcare and behavioral health providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes a mandated general fund appropriation starting in FY 2025 of $25.6 million (and at least $35.5 million annually thereafter) for Maryland Department of Health provider reimbursements. Due to the one-year delay in required employer contributions, State employer expenditures across all funds decrease by $28.7 million in FY 2024 and $10.0 million in FY 2025. Programmatic special fund revenues and benefit expenditures for the FAMLI Fund are delayed by one year. Local government employer contributions are also delayed until October 1, 2024.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Labor is the primary regulatory and implementing agency responsible for administering the Family and Medical Leave Insurance (FAMLI) Program, establishing contribution rates, conducting annual cost analyses, adopting regulations, and managing claims, appeals, and fund operations.

The bill mandates that the Maryland Department of Health reimburse certain licensed or certified community service providers for their required employer contributions to the FAMLI Program at least quarterly, resulting in tens of millions of dollars in annual general fund expenditures.

As the state's central budget and personnel agency, DBM oversees state employee benefits and personnel policies. The bill delays required state employer contributions for state employees and establishes mandated general fund appropriations.

The bill assigns the Board of Public Works the statutory duty to annually evaluate state employment data and determine whether to temporarily suspend inflation-based increases to the maximum weekly FAMLI benefit.

The Board of Public Works is authorized by the bill to consider state revenue performance reported by the Office of the Comptroller when determining whether to suspend increases to maximum weekly benefits.
The bill alters statutory check-issuing procedures under § 8.3-505 for paying FAMLI benefits or refunds, eliminating the requirement that checks bear the signature of the State Treasurer.

The bill stipulates that employers providing private plans may satisfy program requirements using insurance policies issued by insurers holding a certificate of authority from the Maryland Insurance Commissioner.
The Secretary of Labor is statutorily required to submit an annual report on the operations, participation rates, and fund status of the FAMLI Program to the Governor.

Licensees may sell alcoholic beverages for on-premises consumption provided food is offered at all times and specific sales proportions are met (at least 50% from golf games, at least 15% from food, and no more than 35% from alcohol).
responsible_party: Frederick County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Miniature golf course businesses in Frederick County, their patrons, and the Frederick County Board of License Commissioners.
fiscal_impact_summary: State Effect: None. Local Effect: Frederick County revenues increase by $1,500 annually beginning in FY 2024 from the issuance of one new license fee ($1,500 annual fee). Enforcement activities can be handled with existing county resources. Small business miniature golf courses that obtain the license may experience increased sales revenue.
